## Definition of length

There are many factors, such as the identification of the source,[[1]](List_of_river_systems_by_length#cite_note-amazon-river-source-1) the identification or the definition of the mouth, and the scale of measurement[[2]](List_of_river_systems_by_length#cite_note-2) of the river length between source and mouth, that determine the precise meaning of "river length". As a result, the length measurements of many rivers are only approximations (see also [coastline paradox](Coastline_paradox "Coastline paradox")). In particular, there seems to exist disagreement as to whether the <Nile>[[3]](List_of_river_systems_by_length#cite_note-britannica-nile-3) or the [Amazon](Amazon_River "Amazon River")[[4]](List_of_river_systems_by_length#cite_note-britannica-amazon-4) is the world's longest river. The Nile has traditionally been considered longer, but in 2007 and 2008 some scientists claimed that the Amazon is longer[[5]](List_of_river_systems_by_length#cite_note-AmazonRiver-5)[[6]](List_of_river_systems_by_length#cite_note-bbc-amazon-6)[[7]](List_of_river_systems_by_length#cite_note-inpe-7) by measuring the river plus the adjacent [Pará](Par%C3%A1_River "Pará River") estuary and the longest connecting tidal canal.[[8]](List_of_river_systems_by_length#cite_note-britannica-amazon-length-8) A [peer-reviewed](Peer_review "Peer review") article published 2009 in the *International Journal of Digital Earth* concludes that the Nile is longer.[[9]](List_of_river_systems_by_length#cite_note-liu-etal-river-length-9)

Even when detailed maps are available, the length measurement is not always clear. A river may have multiple channels, or [anabranches](Anabranch "Anabranch"). The length may depend on whether the center or the edge of the river is measured. It may not be clear how to measure the length through a lake or reservoir. Seasonal and annual changes may alter both rivers and lakes. Other factors that can change the length of a river include cycles of erosion and flooding, dams, levees, and [channelization](River_engineering#Channelization "River engineering"). In addition, the length of [meanders](Meander "Meander") can change significantly over time due to natural or artificial [cutoffs](Avulsion_(river)#Meander_cutoffs "Avulsion (river)"), when a new channel cuts across a narrow strip of land, bypassing a large river bend. For example, due to 18 cutoffs created between 1766 and 1885, the length of the Mississippi River from [Cairo, Illinois](Cairo%2C_Illinois "Cairo, Illinois"), to [New Orleans, Louisiana](New_Orleans%2C_Louisiana "New Orleans, Louisiana"), was reduced by 351 kilometres (218 miles).[[10]](List_of_river_systems_by_length#cite_note-US-10)

These points make it difficult, if not impossible, to get an accurate measurement of the length of a river. The varying accuracy and precision also makes it difficult to make length comparisons between different rivers without a degree of uncertainty.

The **Mississippi River System**, also referred to as the **Western Rivers**, is a mostly [riverine](Riverine "Riverine") network of the United States which includes the [Mississippi River](Mississippi_River "Mississippi River") and connecting waterways. The Mississippi River is the largest [drainage basin](Drainage_basin "Drainage basin") in the United States.[[3]](Mississippi_River_System#cite_note-MARB-3) In the United States, the Mississippi drains about 59% of the country's rivers.[[4]](Mississippi_River_System#cite_note-Watkins-4)

From the perspective of natural [geography](Geography "Geography") and [hydrology](Hydrology "Hydrology"), the system consists of the Mississippi River itself and its numerous natural [tributaries](Tributary "Tributary") and [distributaries](Distributary "Distributary"). The major tributaries are the Illinois,[Missouri](Missouri_River "Missouri River"), [Ohio](Ohio_River "Ohio River") and [Red](Red_River_of_the_South "Red River of the South") rivers. Given their flow volumes, major Ohio River tributaries like the [Allegheny](Allegheny_River "Allegheny River"), [Tennessee](Tennessee_River "Tennessee River"), and [Wabash](Wabash_River "Wabash River") rivers are considered important tributaries to the Mississippi system.[[5]](Mississippi_River_System#cite_note-5) Before the Mississippi River reaches the [Gulf of Mexico](Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico"), it runs into its [distributary](Distributary "Distributary"), the [Atchafalaya River](Atchafalaya_River "Atchafalaya River").[[3]](Mississippi_River_System#cite_note-MARB-3)

From the perspective of modern commercial navigation, the system includes the above as well as navigable inland waterways which are connected by artificial means. Important connecting waterways include the [Illinois Waterway](Illinois_Waterway "Illinois Waterway"), the [Tennessee-Tombigbee Waterway](Tennessee-Tombigbee_Waterway "Tennessee-Tombigbee Waterway"), and the [Gulf Intracoastal Waterway](Gulf_Intracoastal_Waterway "Gulf Intracoastal Waterway"). is maintained by the [U.S. Army](U.S._Army "U.S. Army") [Corps of Engineers](U.S._Army_Corps_of_Engineers "U.S. Army Corps of Engineers") with a project depth of between 9–12 ft (2.7–3.7 m) to accommodate [barge](Barge "Barge") transportation, primarily of bulk commodities.[[6]](Mississippi_River_System#cite_note-6)

The Mississippi River carries 60% of U.S. grain shipments, 22% of oil and gas shipments, and 20% of coal.[[7]](Mississippi_River_System#cite_note-7)
